name: Ashwall ForgeWarden Split-Apron & Sleeves Kit
description:
A heavy split-leg forge apron in charred split-grain synthetic leather — deep brown-black with a surface texture of small overlapping scales pressed into the hide during tanning. The bib reaches mid-chest, secured by adjustable neck and waist straps with quick-release buckles. Matched detachable sleeves run from wrist to upper arm, fastening to a shoulder yoke with industrial snap rings. All edges are double-stitched in heat-resistant aramid thread.

The apron's interior is lined with a thin ceramic-fiber batting that insulates against radiant heat from forge and plasma-arc work. Burn marks, weld spatter scars, and grease stains are universal on worn units — a clean kit reads as brand new or desk-bought.
functionality: Rated for radiant heat, weld spatter, and minor plasma arc flash. Split-leg design allows full leg mobility. Detachable sleeves can be added or removed without removing the apron. Quick-release buckles allow emergency doffing in under four seconds.
what_it_says: You work hot, you work hands-on, and you've got the scars to prove you know what you're doing.
worn_by: blacksmiths and bladesmiths in the Gray Zone craft shops
story_hooks: An old apron in a secondhand stall has a name stamped into the bib leather — it belongs to a forge worker who died in a plant fire six months ago, officially ruled an accident.
A batch of ForgeWarden kits was manufactured with ceramic liner batting that's 40% thinner than spec — someone at Ashwall signed off on the substitution.
A master welder refuses to break in a new apron, insisting her twenty-year-old unit carries luck — someone wants it badly enough to offer three times its value.

physical_description.visual_profile: Heavy-duty forge worker's kit with serious industrial presence. The split-leg apron creates a dramatic silhouette—asymmetrical, functional, and visibly scarred from heat work. Detachable sleeves add modularity and suggest someone who values quick gear swaps. Overall impression: blue-collar, heat-hardened, no-nonsense.
physical_description.fit: Relaxed and deliberately spacious through the torso for layering and heat dissipation. Sleeves are snug at the wrist but loose through the forearm to allow glove wear and arm movement. Apron sits low on hips with split legs for stride freedom—designed for standing, bending, and reaching in a forge environment.
physical_description.primary_material: Charred split-grain synthetic leather (petroleum-derived ballistic composite), ceramic-fiber batting lining
physical_description.texture: Scaled surface texture—small overlapping pressed patterns across the hide creating visual and tactile grip. Surfaces are intentionally rough to resist slipping when wet or oily. Seams are thick and visible, reinforced with aramid thread that has a slightly raised, cordlike appearance.
physical_description.color_scheme: Deep brown-black gradient, darker at edges from heat exposure and handling. Visible surface discoloration in spatter patterns—silver weld marks, carbon streaks, grease burnish marks that age into the leather. New units are uniformly dark; worn ones are a palimpsest of work.
physical_description.closures: Quick-release buckles on neck and waist straps (industrial-grade, likely magnetic or friction-lock). Industrial snap rings on shoulder yoke connecting sleeves—loud, mechanical, audible when fastening.
distinctive_features: Split-leg design for mobility and heat escape
Double-stitched aramid seams throughout (heat-resistant, visible as thick raised lines)
Detachable sleeve system via shoulder yoke—modular for different tasks
Ceramic-fiber batting visible at edges and seams (white-cream colored contrast)
Burn marks, weld spatter scars, and grease stains as badges of authentic use
Neck and waist straps with quick-release buckles for emergency removal
Heavy, substantial weight and drape suggesting protective capability
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 3–4 functional. Quality gear for serious industrial work, not luxury. Cost is practical, not aspirational. Ashwall is a workhorse brand, not a corpo prestige label.
physical_description.cultural_context: Worn by forge workers, plasma-arc welders, manufacturing technicians, possibly some military fabrication crews. Signals expertise in heat-work, blue-collar pride, and practical toughness. Wearing clean, unworn Ashwall reads as inexperience or desk-bound posturing.
physical_description.condition_typical: Weathered and scarred. Burns, spatter, grease, carbon residue, and patched repairs are the norm. A pristine Ashwall kit is a red flag—either brand new or never actually used in a forge. Veteran workers' kits show visible layering of damage and repair.
